question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the project life cycle from the software (systems) development life cycle?
options: The project life cycle covers all the activities of the project, while the software development life cycle focuses on realising the product requirements
The project life cycle covers only coding and testing, while the software development life cycle includes initiation and closure
They are the same thing; 'software development life cycle' is simply the Agile name for the project life cycle
The software development life cycle covers all the activities of the project, while the project life cycle focuses on realising the product requirements

question: In which two stages of the five-stage project life cycle does the software development life cycle usually take place?
options: Planning and executing
Executing, and monitoring and controlling
Monitoring and controlling, and closure
Initiation and planning

question: Which sequence lists the five stages of the project life cycle in the correct order?
options: Initiation, executing, planning, monitoring and controlling, closure
Planning, initiation, executing, monitoring and controlling, closure
Initiation, planning, executing, closure, monitoring and controlling
Initiation, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, closure

question: Which description of the waterfall method is correct?
options: Iterative: the same phases repeat in short cycles, each producing a working piece of software
Linear: the phases happen one at a time and you cannot go back to a previous phase
Parallel: all of the phases happen at the same time across different teams
Linear: the phases happen one at a time, but you can freely return to an earlier phase whenever requirements change

question: Under a waterfall approach, a client asks for a change halfway through because a competitor has moved on. What is the typical response?
options: Finish the current project first, then look at the new requirement in the next one
Pause the current phase and update the requirements immediately so the project can adapt
Ask the product owner to re-prioritise the product backlog straight away
Add the change to the next sprint backlog and carry on

question: Which of these was NOT given as a reason the waterfall method was used so widely?
options: It produced detailed documentation that was passed from one phase to the next
It provided predictability
It welcomed new requirements late in development without any renegotiation
It gave a clear timeline and set of deliverables for each phase

question: Which situation was waterfall described as being well suited to?
options: A team using flexible, modern tools with no requirement for formal documentation or long-term planning
A team that wants to demonstrate working software to customers every two weeks and adapt to their feedback
A small start-up with a flat structure whose priorities change every few weeks and which has few formal processes
A regulated industry such as aerospace, defence or finance, or a hierarchical organisation with formal processes

question: What does the training say about Royce, who outlined the waterfall method around 1970?
options: He invented waterfall in the 1980s and 1990s as a response to the rise of iterative approaches such as Agile
His original outline allowed going back to earlier phases, but this was largely ignored as waterfall became rigid
His original outline was strictly linear, and later teams added the ability to go back to earlier phases
He designed waterfall so that operations and deployment would happen continually throughout the project

question: Why was DevOps not really essential when the waterfall method was used?
options: Operations comes at the end, so the software is deployed once and does not need continual automated deployments
Waterfall projects never deploy their software, so there is no operations stage or automation to build
Waterfall teams only produce documentation and specifications, so there is no software to deploy at all
Waterfall already deploys every night by hand, so there is nothing left for DevOps engineers to automate

question: Why did DevOps become relevant shortly after Agile came into being?
options: Agile forbids automation so that individuals and interactions are always put ahead of processes and tools
Agile produces incremental code changes and new versions continually, which need to be deployed continually and automatically
Agile replaces operations teams, so DevOps engineers take over the testing and the product backlog
Agile projects deploy the software only once, at the very end, so deployment has to be right first time

question: In the story of the two-year waterfall project, what went wrong when all the parts were finally put together at the end?
options: The documentation for the different phases had been lost when the work was handed between teams
The parts were built on incompatible architectures, so the application could not work and could not be fixed
The testers ran out of budget before they could run the acceptance tests on the combined system
The customer changed the contract during the final phase and refused to pay for the finished work

question: Which analogy correctly matches each approach to the football-goal example?
options: Waterfall is one shot at the goal from 100 metres away; Agile is taking one step at a time and adjusting as the goalposts move
Both approaches take one step at a time, but Agile keeps the goalposts fixed
Agile is one shot at the goal from 100 metres away; waterfall is taking one step at a time and adjusting as the goalposts move
Waterfall adjusts its aim after every shot, while Agile takes a single shot at the end

question: Which pair of words best describes the Agile approach to the software development life cycle?
options: Iterative and incremental
Incremental and sequential
Linear and incremental
Iterative and linear

question: Which sequence best describes one cycle of the iterative approach?
options: Code, test, plan, design, check, then release everything once the backlog has been emptied
Plan, design, code, test, check, then stop and wait until the end-of-project release
Design, code, plan, check, test, then go around again with the same set of features
Plan the next features, design, code, test and check them, then go around again with the next set

question: When can the waterfall method still be the perfect solution for the software development life cycle?
options: When stakeholders only discover what they want after seeing the product working
When the product is novel, with nuance that will need constant feedback
When the customer wants a working increment every two weeks to review
When the requirements are known at the start, detailed, and not going to change

question: Which project would be the LEAST suited to waterfall?
options: A government project that needs detailed documentation and justified spending at every phase
A novel product where stakeholders will keep changing their minds as they see it
A repeat of a project the company has delivered many times, with fixed requirements
A regulated finance system whose specification is fully known and documented before starting

question: When does working software normally first become available in waterfall compared with Scrum?
options: Both: only at the end of the whole life cycle, once every phase has been signed off
Waterfall: at the end of every sprint. Scrum: at the end of the final phase of the project
Waterfall: at the end of every phase. Scrum: only once, at the end of the whole project
Waterfall: at the end of the whole life cycle. Scrum: at the end of every sprint, as a working increment

question: What is the relationship between Agile and Scrum?
options: Agile is a framework made of ceremonies, artifacts and roles, and Scrum is one of its values
Agile does not specify how to work day to day; Scrum is a framework that gives a way to implement it
Scrum defines the 12 principles, and Agile defines the sprints
Scrum is the Agile manifesto, and it specifies a two-week sprint

question: How many values and principles make up the Agile manifesto?
options: Twelve values, supported by twelve principles
Twelve values, supported by four principles
Four values, supported by four principles
Four values, supported by twelve principles

question: Which statement correctly reflects one of the four Agile values?
options: Processes and tools are valued over individuals and interactions
Individuals and interactions are valued over processes and tools
Comprehensive documentation is valued over working software
Following a plan is valued over responding to change

question: Customer collaboration is valued over what, according to the manifesto?
options: Following a plan
Contract negotiation
Comprehensive documentation
Processes and tools

question: A team spends three weeks writing detailed documentation for a feature but has no working software to show. Which Agile value does this go against most directly?
options: Responding to change over following a plan
Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
Working software over comprehensive documentation
Customer collaboration over contract negotiation

question: Why does the manifesto value individuals and interactions over processes and tools?
options: Processes and tools were the priority in waterfall; they still have value, but people matter more
Processes and tools were only invented after Agile and so are not yet proven to be effective
Agile teams are not allowed to use processes or tools because they slow individuals down
Individuals work best alone, so interactions should be kept to a minimum to avoid slowing delivery

question: What does 'X over Y' mean in the four Agile values?
options: The item on the right must be removed from the project
The item on the right is only needed when using Scrum
Both have value, but the item on the left is valued more
The item on the left replaces the item on the right entirely

question: A customer asks for a change to a feature. In an Agile approach, what matters most?
options: Understanding why the customer wants it and what they really need, then working out how to deliver it
Recording the request carefully and addressing it only after the current project has closed
Renegotiating the whole contract and budget before any of the work is allowed to change direction
Refusing the change politely, because the original plan was agreed and signed at the start

question: Complete the first principle: 'Our highest priority is to satisfy the customer through ____ delivery of valuable software.'
options: continuous but infrequent
early and final
early and continuous
complete and final

question: At a sprint review, a stakeholder sees the product and asks for changes. Which principle does this show?
options: Welcome changing requirements, even late in development
Working software is the primary measure of progress
Business people and developers must work together daily throughout the project
Continuous attention to technical excellence and good design enhances agility

question: What time scale does the principle on delivering working software frequently describe?
options: From a couple of days to a couple of weeks, with a preference for the longer time scale
From a couple of months to a couple of years, with a preference for the shorter time scale
From a couple of weeks to a couple of months, with a preference for the longer time scale
From a couple of weeks to a couple of months, with a preference for the shorter time scale

question: Which two groups must work together daily throughout the project, according to the principles?
options: Sponsors and testers
Business people and developers
The product owner and the project manager
Testers and the Scrum Master

question: A developer picks up a user story that has acceptance criteria, but still has questions about it. What does this show?
options: Developers and business people must keep communicating, so questions still arise even with acceptance criteria
The product owner must now rewrite the whole product backlog before any more stories are started
The developer should save the question for the sprint review, since the story is already in the sprint
The story must have failed its definition of ready, so the whole sprint has to stop immediately

question: Which Scrum event gives people a daily chance to ask for the support they need, in line with building projects around motivated individuals?
options: Sprint planning
The sprint retrospective
The daily scrum (stand-up)
The sprint review

question: A student argued that 'face-to-face conversation' can be virtual. Why is that acceptable?
options: What matters is being able to see each other, including body language, which is why cameras are on
Only meetings with stakeholders need to be face-to-face; team conversations can be text only
Written messages convey information just as efficiently as speaking, so cameras are optional
Face-to-face only applies to sprint planning, where the whole team must be physically present

question: Which of the three C's of a user story is most closely linked to face-to-face communication?
options: Card
Collaboration
Conversation
Confirmation

question: Is working software only available at the end of a sprint?
options: Yes, working software only exists once the sprint review has been held and the stakeholders have signed it off
Yes, working software only exists at the end of the final sprint, once the product goal is reached
No, but only the product owner may declare a piece of software to be working before the sprint ends
No, some teams have working software daily, for example via version control, even if it is not yet the end product

question: Which statement matches the principle on sustainable development?
options: Sprints should get shorter each time so that delivery speeds up as the project goes on
Only developers need a constant pace, while the sponsors can vary theirs as they choose
Teams should work at maximum pace early on and slow down towards the end of the project
Sponsors, developers and users should be able to maintain a constant pace indefinitely

question: Several team members mention separate blockers at the daily scrum, but they all trace back to the same underlying issue in the product backlog. What does this suggest?
options: Things are not sustainable and the underlying issue needs reviewing
Each blocker is independent, so nothing needs to change
The sprint should be extended so everyone can catch up
The Scrum Master should replace the blocked team members

question: Which pillars were used to show 'continuous attention to technical excellence and good design enhances agility' in action?
options: Transparency (facts are shared), then adaptation (the manager fixes the issue)
Adaptation (everyone checks what is released), then transparency (the team improves)
Inspection (everyone checks what is released), then adaptation (the team improves)
Transparency (everyone checks what is released), then inspection (the team improves)

question: Why are the Agile principles called principles rather than rules?
options: They are enforced by the Scrum Master and must be applied identically by every team using Scrum
They only apply to teams using Scrum, and they cannot be adapted to the way a team works
They can be applied in many ways; new teams follow them strictly, while experienced teams gain flexibility
They are optional for every team unless a regulator requires that they are followed in full

question: Daria saw principle 1 in prototyping during requirements gathering and in the increment produced each sprint. Which part of the principle did each show?
options: Prototyping showed 'continuous' delivery; the increment each sprint showed 'early' delivery
Both showed only 'continuous' delivery
Prototyping showed 'early' delivery; the increment each sprint showed 'continuous' delivery
Prototyping showed 'valuable' software; the increment showed 'early' delivery

question: Who is the go-to person for understanding the product the team is building (what it needs to do and how it should work)?
options: The product owner
The most senior developer
The project manager
The Scrum Master

question: Which of these is the product owner accountable for?
options: Chairing the daily scrum and coaching the team on how the Scrum framework should be followed
Deciding which developer works on which task in the sprint and tracking each person's progress
Managing the product backlog, including its content, its availability and its order
Managing the sprint backlog and deciding mid-sprint what the team should be working on

question: A key stakeholder meets the product owner mid-sprint and explains a new feature that now matters more than others. What should the product owner update?
options: The product backlog, so the new priority is visible at the next sprint planning
The sprint backlog, so the team switches to the new feature straight away
Both backlogs, so that the change takes effect immediately in the sprint
Neither backlog; the change waits until the sprint review to be recorded

question: Why would the product owner not change the sprint backlog in the middle of the sprint?
options: It was decided at sprint planning; changes wait for the next planning meeting, where the product backlog is reviewed
The sprint backlog is owned by the Scrum Master, who is the only person who is allowed to edit it
The sprint backlog can only be reviewed by the stakeholders at the retrospective, not changed by anyone
The sprint backlog is generated automatically from the burn down chart, so it cannot be edited by hand

question: What kind of person is the product owner usually?
options: The most experienced developer on the team, who also chooses the technical design for each story
The tester with the most Scrum experience, who also writes the acceptance tests for each story
A business-type person with deep product knowledge, who may also have some technical experience
A project manager from outside the team who assigns the daily tasks and tracks time and budget

question: Who can cancel a sprint, and under what circumstances?
options: Only the product owner, if the sprint goal has become obsolete
The Scrum Master, whenever the team is falling behind
Any stakeholder, if the sprint goal becomes obsolete
The development team, if the stakeholders request it at the review

question: After a sprint is cancelled because its goal is obsolete, what happens next?
options: The team moves into another sprint planning meeting to plan the next sprint
The team waits for the next project to be initiated and then starts again
The team continues the cancelled sprint without a goal until it finishes
The Scrum Master rewrites the product goal alone and restarts the same sprint

question: Which description fits the Scrum Master?
options: The deputy product owner, who prioritises the backlog
The boss of the team, who tells people what to do
A servant leader, facilitator and coach rather than a manager
The lead developer, who decides the technical design

question: What is the Scrum Master's main job?
options: Deciding which developer takes which user story and monitoring how quickly each one finishes it
Writing every user story and keeping the product backlog in the right priority order
Making sure the Scrum processes are followed and removing impediments and blockers from the team
Approving each finished user story before it moves to done and signing it off with stakeholders

question: Who decides who does which task in a Scrum team?
options: The product owner assigns tasks to individuals, based on who knows each feature best
The Scrum Master allocates the tasks to individuals each morning at the daily scrum
The project manager assigns tasks to individuals at the start of the sprint and tracks them
The team works it out together, with people suggesting or volunteering for tasks

question: How is a Scrum Master usually selected?
options: Because they are the most technically experienced developer and so can review all of the code
Because they have been with the company the longest and know how the departments are organised
For their experience in how Scrum is supposed to work, not for being the best coder
Because the stakeholders nominate them at the sprint review, based on how well the sprint went
